gen_risks.description: Training institutions lack adequate equipment, infrastructure and staff, limiting the quality and scale of technical training.
gen_risks.mitigation: Allocate funds for equipment upgrades, refurbish facilities, recruit qualified instructors and provide continuous professional development.
gen_risks.evidence: capacity remains constrained by outdated equipment, limited infrastructure, insufficient operating budgets, staffing gaps (Section 12).

gen_risks.description: Curricula may not match employer needs, leading to skills mismatches and low graduate employability.
gen_risks.mitigation: Establish regular employer advisory panels, embed employer‑driven competency standards in curricula, and monitor placement outcomes.
gen_risks.evidence: most firms perceive that the education and training systems do not adequately prepare youth (Section 11).

gen_risks.description: Floods, storms and landslides could damage training facilities and disrupt program delivery.
gen_risks.mitigation: Incorporate climate‑resilient design in renovations and new construction, and develop contingency plans for temporary relocation of activities.
gen_risks.evidence: STP is vulnerable to coastal and riparian floods, severe storms, landslides (Section 4).

gen_risks.description: Delays in financial reporting and internal audits may hinder timely disbursements and compliance.
gen_risks.mitigation: Appoint an experienced accountant, customize accounting software for real‑time reporting, and enforce strict audit timelines.
gen_risks.evidence: delays in recording financial transactions and generating financial reports; internal audit reviews not timely (Section 56).

gen_risks.description: Weak coordination between AFAP and ministries could slow procurement of goods and services.
gen_risks.mitigation: Create joint procurement task‑forces with clear SOPs and shared timelines, and hold weekly coordination meetings.
gen_risks.evidence: ability of AFAP and the MLSSS to work in close collaboration is key for timely procurement (Section 57).

gen_risks.description: Risk of sexual exploitation, abuse or harassment affecting especially female trainees and interns.
gen_risks.mitigation: Hire dedicated GBV/SEA specialists, implement strict code of conduct, provide safe reporting channels and conduct regular awareness trainings.
gen_risks.evidence: require hiring Environmental Specialist with SEA/SH expertise; risks of sexual exploitation and abuse (Legal covenants).

gen_risks.description: Beneficiary selection may exclude marginalized groups or be captured by elites, undermining equity goals.
gen_risks.mitigation: Use transparent, data‑driven targeting from the Unique Social Registry, and establish independent oversight of selection processes.
gen_risks.evidence: risks of exclusion, especially for marginalized groups, if benefits not equitably distributed (Section 58).

gen_risks.description: The new labor market information system may not become fully functional, limiting data‑driven employment services.
gen_risks.mitigation: Adopt a phased rollout with pilot testing, allocate dedicated IT staff, and secure vendor support for system maintenance.
gen_risks.evidence: Employment Observatory never fully operationalized; new system may not be operational (Sections 32‑33).

gen_risks.description: CERC may not be activated promptly during a crisis, delaying reallocation of funds to vulnerable beneficiaries.
gen_risks.mitigation: Finalize the CERC manual before effectiveness, train staff on activation procedures, and conduct tabletop simulations annually.
gen_risks.evidence: CERC manual to be prepared after effectiveness; staff orientation required (Section 47).

gen_risks.description: Insufficient partnerships with overseas employers could limit labor‑mobility opportunities for youth.
gen_risks.mitigation: Negotiate MoUs with destination‑country employers, leverage CPLP networks, and showcase qualified candidates through the Employability Portal.
gen_risks.evidence: explore partnerships with relevant overseas employers to advertise opportunities (Section 34).

gen_risks.description: Limited grant and scholarship budgets may fall short of the target numbers of beneficiaries.
gen_risks.mitigation: Monitor disbursement pace quarterly, re‑prioritize allocations if needed, and seek supplemental donor contributions.
gen_risks.evidence: project finances 0.00 financing gap but grant amounts limited; risk of not meeting 1,000 scholarships (Section 44).

gen_risks.description: Cultural and time‑poverty constraints may prevent women from reaching the 50 % participation target.
gen_risks.mitigation: Provide childcare services at training sites, schedule flexible class times, and conduct gender‑sensitive outreach through women’s associations.
gen_risks.evidence: women face higher poverty, lower labor participation; project aims 50 % women but barriers exist (Sections 9, 23).

gen_risks.description: Private sector firms may not actively engage in Workforce Development Committees, reducing relevance of training programs.
gen_risks.mitigation: Offer incentives such as partial compensation for training slots and public recognition for participating firms.
gen_risks.evidence: Workforce Development Committees bring together private sector employers; participation may be limited (Section 27).

gen_risks.description: Logistical challenges of delivering equipment and staff to Príncipe could delay construction of the new training centre.
gen_risks.mitigation: Develop a detailed logistics plan, secure local transport contracts early, and build buffer time into the construction schedule.
gen_risks.evidence: Príncipe is 170 km away, geographically isolated, with limited skilled workers (Section 1).

gen_risks.description: Weak monitoring and evaluation data quality could impede learning and evidence‑based adjustments.
gen_risks.mitigation: Implement standardized data collection tools, train staff on M&E protocols, and conduct periodic data quality audits.
gen_risks.evidence: monitoring includes spot checks; risk of weak data if not properly managed (Section 51).

gt_risks.description: Frequent government changes and the cross-ministerial nature of the jobs agenda can shift policy direction, counterpart arrangements, and implementation momentum; further changes may follow the mid-2026 legislative/parliamentary elections. Success depends on sustained coordination across labor, education, tourism, agriculture, and finance ministries plus private-sector engagement.
gt_risks.mitigation: Anchor the project within MLSSS (core employment-promotion mandate); strengthen technical ownership at directorate level rather than relying on political leadership; establish a formal coordination committee and a unified PIU; continue policy dialogue with Government during implementation.

gt_risks.description: STP's fragile growth outlook, narrow fiscal space, and dependence on external financing leave it highly vulnerable to external shocks (energy/food price swings, donor-disbursement delays, climate events), which may weaken labor demand, reduce firms' absorption capacity, and constrain the Government's ability to sustain recurrent-cost interventions (training, stipends, employment services).
gt_risks.mitigation: Prioritize low-cost, scalable interventions; combine supply-side investments with direct job-creation support; target sectors with growth potential and external demand linkages (incl. labor mobility); coordinate with other World Bank macro-fiscal/energy/private-sector engagements in STP.

gt_risks.description: Limited experience of MLSSS and DTEFP in delivering complex labor-market interventions at scale; fragmented institutional landscape; multiple implementation partners; nascent capacity in labor-market analytics, employment intermediation, and cross-sectoral coordination; sustainability risk if new systems/programs are not institutionalized within government structures and budgets.
gt_risks.mitigation: Leverage existing institutions/mechanisms rather than parallel structures (existing MLSSS PIU, coordination committee, AFAP for fiduciary/safeguards); finance targeted TA and staffing; invest in durable institutional assets (labor-market information system, employability portal, strengthened training institutions, formalized service-provider arrangements); use the learning agenda and impact evaluation to identify cost-effective interventions for scale-up.

gt_risks.description: Complex procurement in a small-island context: residual FM risk is moderate but residual procurement risk is substantial, driven by the complexity of civil works in a remote island context, the large number of technical-assistance contracts, and the multiplicity of projects already handled by AFAP.
gt_risks.mitigation: Agree ToRs and technical specifications between AFAP and the World Bank before initiating any procurement (prior and post-review); reinforce AFAP procurement and contract-management capacity incl. specialized support for civil-works supervision; embed dedicated fiduciary controls for the grants/stipends payment mechanism in the Project Operations Manual; continue and adapt the risk assessment during implementation.
